opus-5.5.text:
It's one of the things I find most beautiful about olfaction, honestly. When you smell something, you're not detecting light that bounced off it or a pressure wave it sent through the air. You're literally taking a little piece of that thing into your body. Molecules that were part of a flower, or a loaf of bread, or another person, are physically binding to receptors in your nose. It's an incredibly intimate sense in that way.

And I think that's part of why smell is so tied to emotion and memory. Anatomically, the olfactory system has this very direct line into the parts of the brain that handle emotion and memory, the amygdala and hippocampus, without some of the relay stations the other senses go through. So the experience of smelling someone you love, a partner, a child, a parent, carries this immediacy that's hard to put into words. People will keep a loved one's sweater after they pass away, not for how it looks, but because it still smells like them. That's a physical trace of a living person you can still connect with.

It also goes beyond humans. Much of the living world communicates chemically. Plants signal to each other and to insects with volatile compounds. Animals mark territory, find mates, and recognize kin through smell. So when we smell, we're tapping into what's probably the oldest communication channel life has. Bacteria were sensing chemicals long before anything had eyes or ears.

For me, working on digitizing smell, that's part of the motivation. It's a sense that connects us so deeply to each other and the natural world, yet we've had almost no tools to understand, measure, or share it the way we can with images or sound. If we can give computers a sense of smell, I think we'll understand that connection a lot better, and maybe use it to help people, whether in detecting disease, protecting food supplies, or just appreciating the world around us more richly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really beautiful about olfaction, and it's a little bit of a mind-bender when you first sit with it. When you see something, photons bounce off of it and hit your retina. When you hear something, pressure waves move through the air and vibrate your eardrum. There's always this intermediary. But when you smell something, actual pieces of that thing are physically entering your body. Molecules that were, moments ago, part of a flower or a loaf of bread or another person are now floating up into your nasal cavity, binding to receptors that are, in a very literal sense, part of your brain. The olfactory neurons are the only place where the central nervous system is directly exposed to the outside world.

So when you smell your partner, or your kid, or your dog, you're not perceiving a representation of them at a distance. Little bits of them are inside you, touching your nervous system. I think that's part of why smell is so tied to memory and emotion, why it feels so intimate and so hard to put into words. It's less like observing and more like a chemical handshake.

And from a scientific standpoint, that's also what makes it so hard. The input isn't a wavelength or a frequency, it's the structure of molecules, and there are hundreds of millions of possible ones. We have roughly four hundred different receptor types, and we still don't have a map from chemistry to perception the way we do for color or pitch. So the thing that makes smell the most physically direct sense is also the thing that's kept it the least understood. That's a big part of what drew me to it.

astra-6.text:
There’s something really intimate about smell. For you to smell another living thing, molecules have to leave its body, travel through the air, and enter your nose. So you’re actually making physical contact with a little piece of that organism, even at a distance.

And those molecules carry information. They’re a consequence of what that organism is doing—its metabolism, what it’s eating, its state. I think that’s a beautiful way to think about smell: it connects your nervous system directly to the chemistry of another living thing.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s something really intimate about smell. For you to smell another living thing, molecules from that organism have to travel through the air, enter your nose, and interact with receptors in your body. So there’s this literal material connection. You’re not just observing it from a distance; a little piece of its chemistry is reaching you.

And those molecules can carry information about what’s happening inside that organism. We don’t necessarily know how to interpret all of it, but I find that remarkable: the air around us contains these chemical signals, and our sense of smell gives us access to some of them.
